name: PCB Assembly

claims.claim_text: A production assembly line runs as a conveyor sequence: solder paste applied by machine through a stencil, pick and place, an optional human inspection station before reflow whose operator looks at the board without touching it to catch catastrophic errors, the reflow oven, a further quality check, automated optical inspection, then through-hole placement, which remains manual because it has not been automated in most shops, and finally automated functional test fixtures and flying-probe testing.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes they'll have in a good shop, they'll have someone between the pick and place machine and the, uh, and the reflow oven
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Reel loading onto the feeders is the step that has stayed manual even in well-automated shops, so the visible difference between a good factory and a poor one is that in the good one people watch machines rather than handle boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've never seen a automated reel loading
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Mechanised through-hole soldering repays its cost even where labour is cheap, on reliability grounds rather than labour cost: a line built in a low-wage location started with people doing through-hole work and moved to machines because the mechanised process was more consistent.
claims.quote_verbatim: we find that the reliability of mechanized through-hole soldering is such that automation really pays off
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Stencil printing is a single-shot deposition of paste across an entire board or panel, which is what makes it repeatable at volume; the alternative of jetting paste pad by pad rasters across the board and takes far longer per unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a single shot exposure for an entire board versus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Production stencils are mounted in frames that hold the foil under high tension in a small number of standard sizes, typically 23 by 23 or 29 by 29 inches with tubular or slim frame profiles, so that the stencil lands in the same position on every board and the deposition is consistent.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're pulled extremely tight
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Where a design is entirely in stock, both bare boards and components, an assembly house can turn a build in about twenty-four hours; the same absence of waiting is what distinguishes board assembly from semiconductor packaging, where prefabricated dies and substrates still take weeks.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I've got the green PCB in, in, in stock and I've got all the devices in stock, I can probably build that up in 24 hours

claims.claim_text: Fast-turn assembly services impose a house parts library as the price of the schedule: three-day turnaround is achievable only because the stock is already held and the feeders already programmed for those parts, which removes both external lead time and setup error from the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to be using the open parts library
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: A hybrid model lets a shared facility machine-place the standard parts from its library and then hand the pasted board back to the customer to place unusual components by hand before it goes through the oven, which extends automated assembly to designs the feeders cannot cover.
claims.quote_verbatim: before they actually put the whole thing through the oven, they'll let people come in and hand place
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: An assembly service can hold the component inventory itself and sell only the finished product: it does not sell bare boards and does not sell parts, on the reasoning that stocking the components in-house is what removes external lead time from a prototype order.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only thing we really actually sell is assembled circuit boards
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Board assembly resists the automation levels reached in semiconductor manufacturing because the workpiece is not uniform: circuit boards vary in size and shape, carry large connectors and heavy components, and warp in ways that a wafer does not, so the handling mechanics differ for every job.
claims.quote_verbatim: those circuit boards can all look pretty different, different sizes, shapes
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: The assembler, not the standard, decides the footprint. IPC defines least, nominal and most land patterns for each package according to board density, and an assembly house will nominate the variant its equipment is qualified for on the grounds that it produces the lowest defect rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: our equipment's optimized for this footprint. We know this one works. We trust it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Panelisation must be agreed with the assembler before the panel is drawn, because a panel that a fabricator will make is not necessarily one the placement machine can handle. Inconsistent copper coverage across a panel also causes plating problems that surface as breaks and shorts, to the point where a fabricator may decline the job rather than hand-correct hundreds of defects.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't have, um, consistent copper coverage across your panel, then you're going to have plating issues
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Process differences between suppliers are real and undocumented: what works at one fabricator or assembler may not work at another. Environmental regulation drives some of it, so that in one region a via is plated only if it has copper on both sides, while elsewhere a different resist process plates in a single pass.
claims.quote_verbatim: What might work at one fab doesn't work at another
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Feeder capability constrains what can be sent for assembly at all: an unusually wide part such as a long connector may require a feeder the assembler does not own, so a design cannot simply be handed over on the assumption that any shop can build it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have to buy this special feeder reel that's, you know, two inches wide
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The silkscreen has to carry the information the assembler cannot infer. A part whose polarity is not marked stops the build while the assembler tries to reach the customer, and a late substitution such as a tantalum capacitor for a ceramic one turns an unmarked orientation into a blocked job on hundreds of boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we can't tell what polarity your led is supposed to be
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Pin-one markers placed directly over the pin-one pad, which many CAD libraries supply as the default, conflict with assembly, because the machine needs that pad; the purpose of the whole layout exercise is to get the board built, so assembly constraints govern the footprint.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole driver behind designing a circuit board is to get it assembled
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Assemblers commonly label boards at the end of the run rather than as they are built, so tracing which units received an alternate part requires an explicit instruction to label at that point; otherwise the boards are batched and the distinction is lost.
claims.quote_verbatim: They might apply labels right at the finished end after you've bunched all the boards together
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A bare board and an assembled board are distinct items with distinct part numbers, generated at design time from a product lifecycle management system and printed on the silkscreen so both appear on the board itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: There'll be a part number for the bare PCB. And then there'll be a part number for the assembled PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Ordering from an assembly house needs a three-part identifier because the layers revise independently: the revision of the bare board, the revision of the assembly built on it, and the firmware version programmed at build time.
claims.quote_verbatim: That would be version three of the PCB
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Traceability is built by scanning at each transition: a code on the bare board identifies it, the populated board is tested in an in-circuit fixture and relabelled as an assembly, and the assembly serial numbers are scanned into the finished-unit test report. The record then carries which test fixture and which pogo-pin cassette were used, the timestamps, and whether the board passed first time, so a worn fixture showing rising failures can be identified as the cause.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might scan a QR code on a bare board that identifies which bare board you're using

claims.claim_text: Test rather than assembly dominates the schedule on high-reliability hardware: a satellite programme runs over four hundred unique tests spanning individual printed circuit board assemblies up through vibration and thermal-vacuum on the integrated system, and the test phase is the bulk of a twelve to eighteen month integration period.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's over 400 unique tests that we perform on everything from printed circuit board assemblies
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: Consolidating a product onto one board rather than several is a manufacturing decision as much as an electrical one, because a single board can be tested and calibrated in one fixture, which matters most at batch sizes below tens of thousands.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's way way easier if you can have a single board we can test that single board we can calibrate that single board in one fixture
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Industrial design can force the opposite decomposition: a consumer robot with sensors and indicators positioned on different planes inside its enclosure was built as twelve separate board assemblies joined by wiring harnesses, because that was the practical way to place each element where the geometry required.
claims.quote_verbatim: dash consists of 12 different PCBA assemblies inside of it
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: Board runs of a few hundred sit at an awkward scale where hand assembly consumes whole nights but automated test jigs are only just worth developing, and every unit still has to be verified because downstream users depend on them working.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's that sort of awkward number where you start putting effort into designing, uh, automated test jigs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: The economics of owning a placement machine rarely work for a designer: against roughly five dollars a board to have it assembled, a ten thousand dollar machine must also absorb the time to learn, run, tune and maintain it. The case it genuinely solves is being able to build at any hour on demand, which few people need, and where they do, overnight service from an assembly house is usually faster and cheaper.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do you justify $10,000 pick and place machine and all the infinite amount of time and energy required to run it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The threshold at which in-house placement starts to make sense is not five boards but a few tens, and buying a machine for one's own needs creates an obligation to run other people's boards to justify the purchase.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want to make 25 or 50
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Production placement machines require three-phase power and compressed air and occupy floor space rather than bench space, which is the practical obstacle for anyone contemplating a bench-scale line of stencil station, placement machine and reflow oven.
claims.quote_verbatim: they need like three phase power and, and they need shop air
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Occasional in-house assembly never converges on a repeatable process, because each job starts from scratch: the thermal mass of a board changes with layer count, copper weight and the thermal relief on its pads, so the reflow profile has to be re-established every time.
claims.quote_verbatim: the thermal mass of a PCB can change dramatically
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: The skills decay between builds, paste application most obviously, so an operator who does it rarely does it badly; a machine left unused for six months has to be relearned, which is why four days of setup to build fifty boards compares poorly with four days of hand assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd spend four days Setting up and dicking around with a pick and place machine anyway, probably just to make 50 boards
claims.speaker: Ian Johnston

claims.claim_text: Where a placement service exists that will paste, place and reflow a handful of boards for a day's wages, that is an order of magnitude cheaper than setting up automation for the same three to five boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're paying someone just to do that all day long

claims.claim_text: Shared-facility placement machines need a dedicated operator who does nothing else, and the same holds for board milling machines; equipment that anyone may walk up and use does not produce reliable results.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need somebody who actually runs it

claims.claim_text: Designing a board and assembling it are separate skills, and competent designers frequently never assemble their own work, either from lack of interest or because the time is better spent elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know other engineers that really love designing boards and they design fantastic boards, but like they would never
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Hand assembly is nonetheless useful as a bring-up technique on an untested design, because the board can be populated in sections and each section powered and checked before the rest is fitted, rather than committing the whole board at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: Maybe I don't put all the parts on if I are a part of it, test it, make sure that nothing's going to let the magic smoke out
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Placement is charged per component, at around five to six cents per placement for medium to small volumes, which makes part count rather than board area the cost driver. A design with five hundred parts, as multi-channel analog products tend to have, turns placement into the dominant line item and can justify bringing assembly in-house.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're paying about five or six cents per placement
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: At the other end of the range, a board of roughly a thousand parts across a hundred and thirty distinct line items was assembled offshore for about a hundred dollars a board, at quantities of a few hundred where no meaningful component discounts apply.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's about a hundred dollars assembly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: First-article assembly costs are dominated by setup rather than by the parts, so an order of five boards can cost several hundred dollars; the comparison that matters is not the unit price but the cost and delay of doing it by hand, against which paying the setup is usually worth it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to cost $800 to get the first five boards manufactured
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Setup charges make low-quantity work disproportionately expensive, which is the structural reason a designer who mostly builds small numbers of things hand-assembles even while using assembly houses for the jobs that justify them.
claims.quote_verbatim: set up charges kind of hit you in the, in the gut
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Todd Bailey - Embedded Embrasure Engineering

claims.claim_text: Defects grow more expensive as boards move up the value chain: a fault discovered after four or five thousand boards have been populated cannot be answered by scrapping them at the cost of a bare board, because the parts and the labour are already committed, leaving only rework or scrap at the assembled value.
claims.quote_verbatim: The cost is so, you know, it's not like we can scrap like 4,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A bare-board parameter out of tolerance can present as a mechanical field failure rather than an electrical one: printed circuit board thickness slightly outside specification produced an intermittent rotary range switch on about two percent of units, discovered only after the product had begun shipping.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the thickness of the PCB was slightly out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Failures concentrate in assembly rather than in silicon: solder that does not flow, a joint that does not make contact, a part that is wrong. Integrating a function onto the die therefore maximises the chance of it working at all, at the cost of removing every remedy, since a board allows a trace to be cut or a wire moved and a die does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: things don't go wrong in a chip. Things go wrong in assembly
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: An assembly run cannot start until every part is present, so the constraint that governs scheduling is completeness of the kit rather than the value or difficulty of any individual line.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have all your parts in. Usually they don't assemble boards either
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Automated assembly quoting was the hard part of building an online manufacturing service and required a working partnership with an actual assembly house to calibrate the model. Board cost was approached empirically, starting from a guess and refining it against thousands of real orders until the model predicted the invoice. The resulting ability to quote in minutes is what enables a three-day turnaround from finished design to board in hand, which a conventional contract manufacturer cannot match because it cannot quote in an hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: the assembly side was absolutely the hardest part
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Turnkey services collapse the fabrication and assembly steps into one transaction: design files are synchronised from a folder, Gerbers are generated, parts are matched against a catalogue, the user selects which positions are populated and how many boards are wanted, and the service orders the bare boards, buys the parts and ships the assembled result.
claims.quote_verbatim: They will order your PCB and they will get your PCB manufactured and they'll ship it off to the assembly
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Behind such a service, a single customer order becomes one to three orders placed with fabricators, assemblers and component suppliers with everything drop-shipped to the right place, so that an unassembled order simply arrives as two boxes, one of boards and one of parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: we place between one and three orders with, with manufacturers, assemblers, and suppliers
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Some services push placement verification back onto the customer, who checks component outlines against the Gerbers before the job runs, and bundle several customers' designs onto a shared panel so that the setup cost is shared.
claims.quote_verbatim: you actually verify placement of components using part outlines onto the Gerbers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: Pricing assembly by board area rather than by part count, on the model already used for bare boards, is an alternative structure that shifts the cost driver away from component quantity.
claims.quote_verbatim: just pricing by volume or by area, rather, like so board area, and then applying that to assembly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Selling an assembled board has become cheaper and easier than selling the equivalent kit, because the labour the buyer would have supplied now costs less than the labour of kitting; that reversal is why kits have declined as a product form.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is actually cheaper and easier for me to sell a finished board, a finished fully assembled board than it is to sell the kit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: Supplying parts kits for others to assemble fails on quality: recipients fitted chips and capacitors backwards, and troubleshooting their assembly errors consumed more time than the exercise was worth, which is what drove the move to selling assembled boards instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: They put the chips on backwards and they put the caps in backwards
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: The collapse in bare board and assembly cost changed prototyping method rather than just its price: where point-to-point wiring was once the fast route, laying out a two or four layer board that carries off-the-shelf modules on headers is now both quicker and more repeatable.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's literally faster and cheaper to just do it in a repeatable way using a two layer, four layer PCB
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Building the complex, shared part of a design once as a module and carrying variants on simple two-layer host boards moves the assembly difficulty into a single reusable item, so that changing a sensor becomes a trivial board change and the module itself can be developed by a separate team with the relevant expertise.
claims.quote_verbatim: You kind of centralize the complexity onto the module
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Assembly capacity is unevenly distributed to the point where whole countries have effectively none: one has a single remaining house specialising in high-end military and radio-frequency work, which will build a small two or four layer prototype but at around a thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's one house left in all of this country that i know of and they do high-end
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For a large build destined for a distant market, assembly cost was not the deciding factor: the difference between local and offshore assembly was small, while shipping, logistics and part sourcing dominated, so the work was routed through a distributor with an office in the destination region.
claims.quote_verbatim: The actual assembly cost, there wasn't a huge difference in the actual assembly cost compared to UK assembly
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Live from Serbia with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Some board fabricators bundle components and assembly with a bare board order at no additional charge where the design uses generic parts they already hold, which changes the economics of a design that has been constrained to commodity components.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will give you free connectors, free resistors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Small manufacturers taking assembly in-house inherit a problem that large manufacturers employ specialists to solve. Working out why components do not solder correctly is an entire career in a large organisation, and while defects can be inspected and reworked at small scale, a defect affecting a few percent of a run of thousands cannot be recovered from without consuming the time that was supposed to produce the margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: corporations spend a huge amount of time and money optimizing their manufacturing processes
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A prototype build that has to be done in days is possible but bypasses contract assembly entirely, since arranging an outside build takes five to ten days before anything is made; twenty boards were instead laid out, fabricated overseas overnight and hand-built in-house to meet the date.
claims.quote_verbatim: we couldn't send it out to be contract manufactured because it takes five or 10 days just to arrange that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: A working relationship with an assembler is worth more than the contract terms suggest: asked to deliver early against a fixed external deadline, a shop accepted a partially used reel the customer brought in, re-taped it, ran a hundred and twenty boards ahead of schedule and completed the balance on normal lead time without charging for splitting the run.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually agreed to like take the reel that I had loaded as a partial
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Very small passive packages change what hand assembly means: 0201 parts make 0603 work look comfortable, and modules hand-soldered onto boards during early revisions were moved to professional assembly as soon as the design stabilised.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've ever complained about 0603, just try 0201 for a couple of boards
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: Fine-pitch wafer-level packages are within reach of low-cost fabrication and hand assembly only at the exact process limits: a 0.35 millimetre pitch part required via-in-pad at the minimum permitted 0.25 millimetre spacing, which works only if the layout grid is aligned to it, and not all rows of the package could be escaped. One of three hand-assembled boards came up.
claims.quote_verbatim: the via and pad was the exact amount of uh distance like the the exact minimum distance
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: Stencils ordered alongside a board are made from whichever revision the fabricator processed first and are not revised when the design is, so a stencil can arrive matching an earlier layout; the mismatch is workable when only small parts have moved but has to be anticipated.
claims.quote_verbatim: they made the stencil of the first design and they just they set it and forget it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: A one-person production process is built out of dedicated fixtures rather than general-purpose equipment: a lead-forming machine that cuts and bends component leads to the board, manual insertion, and a solder bath the populated boards are laid onto, with the whole flow specialised to one product at a time.
claims.quote_verbatim: use a, a big solder, uh, bath and, and, and lay these boards on top of the solder bath

claims.claim_text: A hand assembly jig cut to the board outline and 3D printed holds the board flat and supported during paste application, which is the step where a small or irregularly shaped board is otherwise hardest to work with.
claims.quote_verbatim: Made a jig. I was proud of myself for that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
